method: Directly consulted means opened/read at the stated locator or at the precise abstract/record section noted. No abstract, secondary description, or search snippet is represented as a complete scholarly work or primary passage.

episodes.event: Third Council of Constantinople, 680–681; condemnation of monothelitism

sources.type: primary conciliar acts, older English translation
sources.title: Acts of the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681)
sources.exactLocator: Session XVIII definition of faith; Session XIII sentence against monothelites; page's translated act extracts
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened acts and read definition: two natural wills and two natural operations; it names the palace hall Trullus as venue. Also read portions of session XIII and its condemnation of Sergius, Cyrus, Honorius and others. Did not read all eighteen sessions or inspect critical Greek/Latin edition.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Acts are a theological and imperial conciliar self-presentation, not neutral minutes; opening papal legate rhetoric is polemical. The English page combines old translations and headings; exact numbering/chronology should be checked against modern edition. Eighteen-session count and dates are secondary reference facts, not established by the read extracts.
sources.supports: Council's doctrinal definition and the stated venue in palace hall Trullus; contested positions are formally condemned in its own record.
sources.doesNotSupport: An uncomplicated textual-comparison process without theological/political stakes, or projecting later Catholic/Orthodox confessional boundaries onto 680.

sources.title: Richard Price, The Acts of the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681)
sources.exactLocator: Not directly opened in this pass; URL is a research lead only
sources.coverageActuallyRead: None.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: The records deserve a modern critical translation and transmission discussion before production use.
sources.supports: Nothing used from this unconsulted candidate.
sources.doesNotSupport: Exact eighteen-session timetable.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Constantinople is correct and the primary translated definition names the palace hall Trullus. Do not choose a precise current archaeological footprint for that hall based on this text alone. The act records an imperial city/council, not a modern national church boundary.
episodes.recommendation: The doctrinal claim is well supported. Retitle/describe the eighteen sessions as a council proceeding; show its factional arguments and technical terminology as attributed conciliar material, not as the narrator's omniscient neutral verdict.

sources.title: Theophanes, Chronographia, AM 6208–6210
sources.exactLocator: AM 6208–6210; not directly extracted in this pass
sources.coverageActuallyRead: No relevant passage was successfully opened/read here. The existing corpus's AM 6209 locator needs correction/check: siege narrative spans annalistic entries around AM 6208–6210 depending conversion/edition.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Theophanes is a much later Byzantine chronicle drawing on earlier sources. Numerical losses and divine-providence elements are not neutral counts. Arabic and Syriac accounts complicate details, chronology, and Bulgar role.
sources.supports: Only a primary-source lead, not a claim accepted from direct reading in this audit.
sources.doesNotSupport: Casualty totals, precise naval/land blockade geometry, or aid details from unconsulted passage.

sources.exactLocator: Not read in this pass

sources.doesNotSupport: Any specific siege reconstruction.

Winter, famine, fleet, and Bulgar intervention details should be attributed and qualified.

episodes.event: Policies associated with Leo III, conventionally placed c.726–730; beginning and first edict uncertain

sources.title: 'Art and Iconoclasm', Oxford Handbook of Byzantine Studies
sources.exactLocator: Chapter abstract
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read abstract only. It presents common chronology as traceable to 730, if not 726, and says causes/extent remain discussed. Full chapter not opened.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Abstract does not provide detailed source argument; no firsthand Leo III decree cited here.
sources.supports: Chronological caution: c.726–730 rather than a securely dated first imperial edict/event.
sources.doesNotSupport: A dramatic removal of an icon at the Chalke Gate, a specific edict, motive, empire-wide ban, or exact date.

sources.type: museum institutional overview with object/region analysis
sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Iconoclasm'
sources.exactLocator: Sections 'Byzantine Iconoclasm' and 'Iconoclasm in the Southern Provinces'
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read institutional overview. It gives conventional sequence (Hieria 754, Nicaea II 787, renewed policy 815, end 843) while warning extant provincial objects suggest a more complex picture and effects may have been concentrated around Constantinople.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Museum essay is a synthesized scholarly overview, not event-specific primary evidence; it itself emphasizes complexity.
sources.supports: Need to distinguish phases, debate from policy, and imperial evidence from unrelated/locally altered imagery in provinces.
sources.doesNotSupport: A homogeneous century-long icon-smashing campaign or a secure Chalke Gate episode.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Constantinople setting is plausible for imperial policies, but the Chalke Gate story is not documented securely enough to use as a map anchor. Conservators/artisans can be fictional local actors; no named artist's experience or motive is established.
episodes.recommendation: Retain the file's caution. Frame as a period of reported policy debate and uncertainty; do not stage icon destruction as confirmed fact or explain Leo III's motive from silence.

episodes.event: Iconoclast council at Hieria, 754; acts survive largely via opponent's quotation/refutation at Nicaea II

sources.type: primary opponent's conciliar proceedings in modern scholarly record
sources.title: Second Council of Nicaea acts, Session VI (787), refutation of Hieria's Horos
sources.exactLocator: Session VI, 6 October; description/pages 425–546 in Richard Price edition record
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened the academic edition page and read session summary: Tarasios' refutation contains the 754 Horos in divided excerpts; Gregory of Neocaesarea is made to read it, followed by a penitential statement. Not full critical edition text. New Advent candidate page was not directly opened in this pass.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: This is Nicaea II's adversarial presentation, not independent Hieria minutes. The whole original proceedings are not extant as an independent neutral record; use mediated wording. The council was under Constantine V, but the exact title 'ecumenical' was the Hieria participants' own claim and rejected by Nicaea II.
sources.supports: A 754 council issued a definition condemning image veneration; its wording can be reconstructed from the later refutation with explicit mediation.
sources.doesNotSupport: A verbatim, neutral transcript of all Hieria sessions, or direct evidence for every workshop/artisan policy in the empire.

sources.title: 'Gates to Asia Minor: The Harbours of Chalcedon, Chrysopolis, Hiereia and Eutroiu Limen Opposite Constantinople', in The Byzantine Harbours of Constantinople (2021)
sources.exactLocator: Indexed extract on Hiereia palace and harbor identification
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read indexed academic chapter extract: Hiereia/Hieron identification and Fenerbahçe peninsula are discussed; full chapter not read. Indicates Asian shore across from Constantinople, near Chalcedon.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Search extract only; source bibliography/argument requires full reading. Modern identification is archaeological-geographical inference.
sources.supports: Hieria is across the Bosporus/Asian shore, not in Constantinople proper; use only broad geographic context.
sources.doesNotSupport: Precise council hall footprint without full archaeology and chapter.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Hieria is the palace/harbor area on the Asian side near modern Fenerbahçe/Kadıköy, not a generic Chalcedon city-center meeting. The selection's geographyId chalcedon is broad regional shorthand; mark the local site as uncertain. The council's acts are opponent-mediated.
episodes.recommendation: The premise is credible with mediated sourcing made explicit. Avoid fabricating original Hieria dialogue or showing a surviving neutral transcript; any workshop logistics should be bounded fiction around a council, not a claim in the acts.

episodes.event: Second Council of Nicaea, 787; defines defense of images and distinction between veneration and worship

sources.type: primary conciliar acts in translated edition
sources.title: Second Council of Nicaea (787), Session VII definition and conclusion
sources.exactLocator: Session VII Horos/definition and concluding veneration passages
sources.coverageActuallyRead: The existing research audit reports opening and reading these passages; for this collection I rechecked the selection source citation but did not re-extract the whole acts page. Treat that prior noted coverage as limited to definition/anathema/final veneration paragraphs, not all acts.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Council text is a self-justifying conciliar definition against a rival council; translated extract, not critical manuscript apparatus. It sets official doctrine but does not prove uniform immediate compliance across the empire.
sources.supports: Council's position distinguishing honorific veneration of images from latreia/worship due to God alone, and its rejection of iconoclast conclusions.
sources.doesNotSupport: Immediate empire-wide restoration in practice, cessation of all disagreement, or an undifferentiated modern Orthodoxy/Catholic split.

sources.title: Richard Price, The Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787)
sources.exactLocator: Accessible edition record, Sessions IV–VII summary
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read the edition record: session VI on 6 Oct reproduces/refutes Hieria's Horos; session VII on 13 Oct reads/signs Nicaea II definition without recorded discussion. Not full book text.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Bibliographic/summary material only, not the complete critical edition.
sources.supports: Procedural chronology and the fact that Hieria's text reaches us through Nicaea II's refutation.
sources.doesNotSupport: A detailed account of subsequent policy enforcement.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Nicaea is present-day İznik in northwestern Anatolia, across the Sea of Marmara from Constantinople; it is not a Constantinople local map. Current structures cannot be assumed to be the 787 council venue absent archaeological stratigraphy/site evidence. Episode selection correctly names Nicaea, not Constantinople.
episodes.recommendation: Prefer 'defines/affirms veneration in 787' over 'restores' if that word implies universal instant practice. A memory/preservation task is fiction, not evidence that a particular object was displaced/restored at the council.

episodes.event: Irene becomes sole ruler after Constantine VI is blinded/deposed in 797

sources.type: primary chronicle in later translation and prosopographical synthesis
sources.title: Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6289; Prosopography of the Byzantine Empire, Constantine VI entry
sources.exactLocator: PBE Constantine VI entry lines citing Theophanes AM 6289 / Zonaras XV.13.4–6
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened PBE entry and read its source-cited account: conspiracy, removal, return to Constantinople, blinding on 15 Aug 797 and Irene's sole rule; it also lays out conflicting traditions about Constantine's subsequent death and different sources' moralizing allegations. This is a reference synthesis, not Theophanes' full passage.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Theophanes is an iconophile chronicler writing later and has a polemical framework. The PBE notes allegations about Irene's motives and contradictory reports on Constantine's survival/death. Do not state a motive (ambition, cruelty, popular will) as fact. Britannica candidate not opened in this pass.
sources.supports: Irene's takeover and Constantine VI's blinding/deposition in 797 are supported by chronicle tradition; exact date given in Theophanes-derived chronology.
sources.doesNotSupport: That Constantine certainly died immediately; a private motive; a universal public reaction; a planned supply shortage or archive crisis.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Episode is local Constantinople, but PBE places Constantine's brief imprisonment in the Purple Room of the palace; the broader succession context can be city-based. The file's rule against controlling/killing historical persons should prevent any interactive depiction of the blinding.
episodes.recommendation: A bounded dispatch/records episode can discuss dynastic transition. Avoid reenacting violence or attributing Irene's inner motives; label the chronicle as an iconophile source.

episodes.event: Charlemagne receives imperial title in Rome on Christmas 800; Constantinople receives later news

sources.title: Einhard, Vita Karoli Magni 28
sources.exactLocator: Chapter 28, 'Charlemagne Crowned Emperor'
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read chapter 28: says Leo III's Roman troubles brought Charles to Rome, that Charles received titles of emperor/Augustus on 25 Dec 800, and that he disliked/says he would not have entered church had he foreseen papal design. Translation by Samuel Epes Turner (1880); chapters 28 passage read, not whole Vita.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Einhard wrote decades later and says he is Charles's debtor and that the Vita is a memorial/eulogy (preface); his account of Charles' alleged surprise is interested and debated. This passage states Roman emperors' jealousy and embassies/letters but does not name a specific Byzantine protest in 800.
sources.supports: Coronation/title event in Rome, date, later diplomatic correspondence as characterized by Einhard, and Einhard's own claim about Charles' surprise.
sources.doesNotSupport: A contemporaneous Constantinopolitan reaction/dispatch, a precise Byzantine legal response, or treating Einhard's 'surprise' explanation as uncontested fact.

sources.title: Rome, location of papal coronation
sources.exactLocator: Not consulted
sources.coverageActuallyRead: None.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: No need for exact site map in this one-map campaign; don't infer ceremony venue from generic Rome map.
sources.supports: No claim used.
sources.doesNotSupport: No Constantinople local footprint.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: The coronation takes place in Rome, off-map. Anna in Constantinople can only know through subsequent reports or documentary comparison; no direct observation or private Roman speech. New Rome vs Rome is a useful interpretive frame, but avoid claiming this one event instantly changed a settled legal doctrine or produced a known immediate dispatch.
episodes.recommendation: Keep as off-map news and source the Byzantine reception independently. Attribute Einhard's surprise story; do not treat it as fact or make the Constantinople narrator present in Rome.

episodes.event: Irene deposed; Nikephoros I takes power in 802

sources.title: Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6295; Prosopography of the Byzantine Empire, Irene entry
sources.exactLocator: DIR Irene overview, references to Theophanes AM 6295 [802/3]
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened the specialist reference search result / landing content and identified AM 6295 as source locator for deposition; did not extract Theophanes passage itself. Britannia candidate URL not opened. PBE-like exact chronicle entry remains to be read directly.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Theophanes is iconophile and may frame Irene sympathetically; exact chronology uses Byzantine indiction/AM year. Later narratives may moralize usurpation or fiscal policy.
sources.supports: Research lead that Theophanes records Irene's deposition in AM 6295 (802/3). This audit treats the event as plausible but does not claim exact scene evidence.
sources.doesNotSupport: Private motive, a singular handover seal or ceremony, or a precise hour/day from the cited reference lead.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Power shift is in Constantinople; no specific documented seal exchange/site in cited lead. A generic administration scene is an explicitly fictional mechanism. Avoid framing contested succession as a modern constitutional procedure.
episodes.recommendation: Source the relevant chronicle passage directly and independently verify chronology. A transition is supportable broadly, but title/scene details remain unapproved.

episodes.event: Campaign against Bulgaria and death of Nikephoros I, 811; battle site distinct/uncertain relative to Pliska

sources.title: Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6303
sources.exactLocator: AM 6303 / AD 810–811 campaign passage
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read search-indexed opening of the translation: Nikephoros assembled troops from Thrace and opposite-shore themes and marched against Bulgars. The page is a personal blog transcription/translation; complete battle and death passage not read here.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Theophanes' campaign narrative is dramatic and iconophile; compare the independent Chronicle of 811/Scriptor Incertus and Bulgarian evidence. Exact battle footprint is disputed/uncertain. The file's Britannica source is tertiary and not opened.
sources.supports: Nikephoros' campaign against the Bulgars in AM 6303; his army's imperial-scale mobilization.
sources.doesNotSupport: That the emperor died at the archaeological site of Pliska itself; exact route/ambush site; scene-level tactical details or attributed speech.

sources.title: Bulgarian Ministry of Tourism, Pliska archaeological reserve
sources.exactLocator: Official site description for Pliska
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read institutional description: remains of first Bulgarian capital are about 29 km from Shumen and about 2 km from present-day Pliska; it notes the capital was burned by Nikephoros in 811. This is site geography, not proof that the emperor died at the capital.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Tourism ministry summary; archaeological site control only, not battle-topography study.
sources.supports: Pliska as a capital/residential center and broad archaeological location.
sources.doesNotSupport: Precise battlefield or death location.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: The campaign enters Bulgaria and sacks Pliska; Nikephoros' death occurred later during retreat/ambush in a mountain pass according to the chronicle tradition, not securely within the capital's ruins. Keep map label Pliska as a regional operation or move local map toward the uncertain pass; do not map an asserted exact battle footprint.
episodes.recommendation: The selection's own footprint caveat is essential. Separate sack of the capital from emperor's death, and avoid turning Theophanes' highly dramatic death account into eyewitness documentary certainty.

episodes.event: Battle of Versinikia in 813, followed by Michael I's fall and Leo V's accession

sources.title: Theophanes AM 6305; PBE entries for Leo V and Krum
sources.exactLocator: PBE Leo 15 entry, June 813 at Bersinikia; Theophanes AM 6305
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read PBE source-cited summary: Leo was with the Anatolikon army at Bersinikia; Theophanes is a principal source. It notes later narrative versions dispute whether Leo withdrew treacherously or remained while Michael's men fled. Did not open the complete chronicle passage.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Theophanes' account and later chroniclers differ on Leo's conduct, and the later iconoclast conflict could color accounts. Exact site of the Versinikia fortress is not established here; Britannica candidate not consulted.
sources.supports: A defeat at Bersinikia/Versinikia near Adrianople in June 813 and subsequent succession crisis; Leo's presence as a commander.
sources.doesNotSupport: That Leo definitely betrayed Michael, exact fight footprint, or the idea that the battle itself occurred inside Adrianople.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Adrianople (modern Edirne) is the regional anchor, while Versinikia's exact location is uncertain and likely north of the city. A map should be regional or explicitly fictionalized; this is not an urban Adrianople battle. Later reports from the Thracian field are plausible dispatch content, not Anna's direct witness unless dossier dates her there.
episodes.recommendation: Keep defeat and resulting succession crisis, but avoid asserting motives/treachery. The relief/refuge mechanic is fictional civilian response and should be labeled as such.

episodes.event: Renewed imperial iconoclast policy under Leo V; synod/council in 815

sources.title: The Iconoclast Controversy 726–843, Oxford Academic; Metropolitan Museum overview
sources.exactLocator: Met essay section 'Byzantine Iconoclasm'; Oxford chapter abstract was used as citation lead but not opened successfully
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Met essay read directly: it states iconoclasm revived in 815 and condemned in 843, while noting complexity of material evidence. Oxford chapter's title/abstract metadata is the selection's research lead only; full chapter not consulted.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: No contemporaneous synod act from 815 directly consulted. Accounts survive in later iconophile narratives; do not assume a simple continuous empire-wide persecution. The exact motive attributed to Leo V needs dedicated sources and should not be inferred from military events.
sources.supports: A renewed official phase is conventionally dated from 815, after the 787 Nicaea II restoration; later 843 settlement marks end of this renewed phase.
sources.doesNotSupport: An uninterrupted policy since 726, precise workshop closures/archive purges, motives attributed to Leo V, or destruction of every icon.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Synod/imperial policy setting in Constantinople is broadly plausible; no precise synod venue or workshop footprint was verified. Iconoclasm is not synonymous with rejection of all art; caution against projecting a modern mass-destruction program onto incomplete evidence.
episodes.recommendation: Separate first phase (c.726/730–787), interval of official image veneration, and renewed phase (815–843). Treat 815 as an attributed policy event and do not script destruction/archival motives as established facts.

episodes.event: Restoration of image veneration under Theodora and Michael III in 843; later commemoration as Triumph of Orthodoxy

sources.title: 'A change of heart? Theophilos on his deathbed', Byzantine and Modern Greek Studies
sources.exactLocator: Article discussion of Theophanes Continuatus, Pseudo-Symeon, and the 843 council; paragraphs discussing 843 meeting and Theophilos' supposed repentance
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened article and read sections explaining that Theophanes Continuatus and Pseudo-Symeon transmit Theophilos' deathbed repentance through Theodora's address to the 843 council; the modern scholar argues these narratives invent/shape repentance to secure the late emperor's memory and regime legitimacy. Article passage is directly consulted; whole article not read.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: The article's conclusion is a modern source-critical argument; its full notes/whole argument should be read before using as final signoff. It demonstrates precisely why late sources are not eyewitness evidence for the deathbed speech or Theodora's motive.
sources.supports: Theodora's regency and 843 restoration are attested by later sources; subsequent memory was politically/theologically shaped. It strongly cautions against treating the deathbed conversion, secret icons, or private motives as fact.
sources.doesNotSupport: A verbatim speech by Theodora, a private deathbed conversion by Theophilos, a claim he changed his mind, or an intact 843 council transcript from contemporaneous minutes.

sources.title: Prosopography of the Byzantine Empire, Theodora 2
sources.exactLocator: Theodora entry, restoration and imperial seal references
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read indexed entry: after Theophilos' death, Theodora and son assumed empire; restoration proclaimed at assembly; entry cites later Vita Methodii and dated seals from 842/843. This is a reference synthesis, not primary acts.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: The prosopography depends on later narrative witnesses and sigillographic interpretation; original 843 council acts do not survive as a straightforward complete record.
sources.supports: Theodora was regent with Michael III; restoration and John V's replacement by Methodios in 843 are standard reconstruction; seals can control titulature/regency broadly.
sources.doesNotSupport: Precise ceremony sequence, exact words, or Theophilos' repentance.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: This was a local Constantinopolitan settlement, commonly associated with the first Sunday of Lent and public restoration/commemoration. Later icon and liturgical imagery is retrospective (for example, the famous Triumph icon is much later); do not show a 9th-century mosaic returned to its exact former wall without archaeological evidence. The file correctly notes 'Orthodoxy' as source-era commemorative terminology, not modern denominational label.
episodes.recommendation: The broad 843 restoration is supportable, but retain distinction between policy restoration, local council/ceremony reconstruction, and later annual commemoration. Do not attribute Theophilos' deathbed conversion or Theodora's inner motives as fact; explicitly present late narratives as later accounts.

The episode records supply mechanics and titles, not full narrative scripts, so no unprovided dialogue or moment-to-moment scene is approved. Source-critical reading remains incomplete for Theophanes on 717–718, Irene/Nikephoros 802, Pliska 811, Versinikia 813, and the 815/843 acta.
